strengths: Achieves equivariance without computational overhead: Unlike existing equivariant networks, Platonic Transformers maintain standard Transformer efficiency while incorporating geometric constraints—a genuine practical advantage

Sound theoretical framework: Rigorous group-theoretic foundation with formal proofs of end-to-end equivariance (Proposition 1) and novel connection between RoPE and dynamic convolution (Proposition 2)
Comprehensive experimental validation: Diverse benchmarks across vision (CIFAR-10), 3D (ScanObjectNN, QM9), and molecular (OMol25) domains with systematic ablations on symmetry group choices
Principled weight-sharing scheme: Equivariance is achieved through constrained linear layers (Eq. 8) rather than adding complex modules, keeping the architecture elegant and maintainable
Theoretical novelty in attention analysis: Proposition 2 revealing RoPE attention as dynamic convolution with explicit Fourier series representation provides new understanding of attention mechanisms
Practical implementation details: Efficient Cayley table approach for group operations and Fourier domain implementation exploration (Appendix M) demonstrate engineering maturity
weaknesses: Instability with learned keys inadequately analyzed: The paper reports that mixed kernels (learned keys) were 'highly unstable' on QM9/OMol25 but only provides qualitative hypothesis without learning curves, gradient statistics, or rigorous ablations of alternative regularization schemes

Limited novelty: Core contribution is combining existing techniques (RoPE from Su et al. 2024 + group convolutions from Cohen & Welling 2016) rather than introducing fundamentally new equivariance mechanisms

Equivariance broken in practice: CIFAR-10 and ScanObjectNN experiments use APE and external reference frames that violate strict end-to-end equivariance, undermining claims about equivariance benefits on these tasks
Modest empirical improvements on non-equivariant tasks: CIFAR-10 +1.24%, ScanObjectNN +0.8% with discrete symmetry assumptions—insufficient to demonstrate value when true symmetry is absent
Discrete approximation quality not characterized: Using 12/24/60 rotations instead of continuous SO(3) is pragmatic but expressiveness loss is not quantified or analyzed

Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds reported; most results appear to be single runs. QM9 results show suspicious precision (0.010 exactly matching EquiformerV2)

Missing analysis of when equivariance helps: No probing studies to verify learned models actually respect equivariances; no investigation of failure modes when true symmetry doesn't match chosen group; no analysis of learned representations

OMol25 results under short training: Only 22 epochs (Appendix L.2) raises convergence questions; comparison under different computational budgets (120 vs. ~475 hrs) makes advantage assessment difficult

Limited theoretical comparison: Claims that equivariant attention (orientation-dependent) is 'more expressive' than invariant attention lack formal justification; no empirical direct comparison on same tasks

Incomplete presentation of method: Architecture breaks equivariance at final predictions through pooling (Appendix G); interaction between frame-dependent position projection and translation equivariance could be clearer

strengths: Elegant resolution of efficiency-equivariance trade-off: achieves SE(n) approximation equivariance in Transformers with zero additional computational cost through principled weight-sharing

Rigorous mathematical framework with formal equivariance proofs (Propositions 3.1, B.1) and group-theoretic justification; novel connection to dynamic group convolution (Prop 4.1) provides theoretical insight

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation across five diverse domains (CIFAR-10, ScanObjectNN, QM9, OMol25, ProteinMD) with extensive ablations, multiple seeds, error bars, and detailed hyperparameter documentation
True computational parity demonstrated through wall-clock timing (Table 11); parameter reduction via weight-sharing (factor of |G|) with practical linear-time convolutional variant
Thorough reproducibility: promised open-source, clear architectural specs (Table 12), detailed implementation (Appendices E-L), realistic equivariance error analysis (Table 13)
Honest treatment of limitations: acknowledges approximate (discrete) equivariance, uncharacterized extreme-scale performance, and stability trade-offs in design choices (Appendix M)
weaknesses: Empirical gains are modest despite theoretical elegance: QM9 generation validity improves only 1.3 points (97.09%→98.43%), and paper's explanation that 'Transformers learn equivariant tasks better unconstrained at scale' undermines core motivation for adding geometric constraints

Theoretical-practice gap on central claims: (1) Proposition 4.1 equivalence to dynamic convolution assumes no softmax, but actual model uses softmax, making the connection approximate with unclear practical value; (2) claimed SE(n) equivariance is actually discrete approximation (12/24/60 rotations), not true continuous equivariance

Insufficient guidance for practitioners: group selection appears to be trial-and-error (Table 7) with no principled framework; fixed vs. learned keys require different stabilization strategies (QK norm) varying by task; need to 'break symmetry' with APE on some datasets suggests method applicability is limited

Limited comparison to equivariant baselines: most comparisons against standard (non-equivariant) Transformers; for molecular tasks, comparing general-purpose Platonic Transformers to specialized Equiformer variants is unfair; missing comparison to large standard Transformers with SO(3) data augmentation

Scalability concerns: extreme-scale performance uncharacterized; Fourier domain implementation (Appendix O) shows throughput gains only at moderately higher hidden dimensions (Table 14), suggesting poor scaling; ImageNet-1K results (Appendix G) show only parity with 39.9M params, not superiority

Incomplete task analysis: when does equivariance help? ProteinMD shows modest gains (1.80 MSE vs 2.11), QM9 generation gap is small. No failure case analysis or principled framework for predicting when equivariance is beneficial. Regularization effect on non-equivariant tasks under-explored

Brittleness in optimization: learned keys destabilize QM9 training without additional QK normalization (Appendix M); softmax-discretization interactions not analyzed; lack of theoretical understanding of when equivariance helps vs. hurts
